title: The Complete Guide to AI Lease Extraction: From PDF to Structured Data
description: How AI lease extraction works, why commercial leases are harder than other documents, and how CRE teams should evaluate build-vs-buy decisions.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: How does AI lease extraction work?
faq.answer: AI lease extraction uses a single vision-capable AI model that reads the lease PDF end-to-end - no separate OCR step. The AI sees page layout, tables, signatures, and stamps the way a human reviewer does, then extracts 126 named fields against a fixed schema with source references. Three independent passes increase reliability: a primary extraction, an adversarial validation pass that re-reads the PDF to flag errors, and an escalation pass on disputed critical fields.

faq.question: How accurate is AI lease extraction?
faq.answer: Purpose-built AI lease extraction achieves confidence-scored field extraction on standard commercial leases (NNN, modified gross, full service gross) with clean digital PDFs. Ground leases, heavily amended leases, and scanned documents below 200 DPI typically produce more low-confidence fields. Per-field confidence scores identify uncertain extractions so reviewers focus on the fields that need human validation.

faq.question: What makes commercial leases harder to extract than other documents?
faq.answer: Commercial leases present three unique extraction challenges. First, they contain cross-referenced defined terms that change the meaning of common words (e.g., 'Rent' may be defined to include base rent plus CAM plus insurance). Second, amendment chains override base lease provisions, requiring the extraction system to resolve conflicting values across multiple documents. Third, they include complex financial structures (percentage rent, CAM caps, gross-up provisions) that require mathematical understanding, not just text extraction.

faq.question: Should I build or buy lease extraction software?
faq.answer: Build if you process 10,000+ leases per year and need custom field schemas specific to your business. Buy if you process fewer than 10,000 leases per year or need extraction alongside other workflows (due diligence, compliance, portfolio management). The build cost for a production-grade extraction pipeline is $200,000 to $500,000 in engineering time plus ongoing model maintenance. Purpose-built tools like Lextract cost $15 per lease with no upfront investment.

faq.question: Can AI extract data from scanned lease PDFs?
faq.answer: Yes. Modern vision-capable AI reads scanned PDFs natively as images - there is no separate OCR step. It recognizes text, tables, signatures, and stamps the way a human reviewer does. Quality still depends on the underlying visual signal: documents at 300+ DPI extract with stronger confidence, while extremely degraded scans (heavy skew, faded text, deep speckling) reduce confidence on affected fields. Per-field confidence scoring flags those fields so reviewers know which to verify.

title: ASC 842 and IFRS 16: The Complete Lease Data Requirements Guide
description: A field-by-field reference for the lease data your accounting team needs to comply with ASC 842 and IFRS 16.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: What lease data do I need to collect to comply with ASC 842?
faq.answer: At minimum you need the lease commencement date, lease term, lease classification (finance vs. operating), fixed payment amounts and escalation schedule, variable payment components, options to extend or terminate (and whether exercise is reasonably certain), and the incremental borrowing rate used to discount the liability. Missing even one of these fields produces an incorrect right-of-use asset or lease liability calculation.

faq.question: What is the difference between a finance lease and an operating lease under ASC 842?
faq.answer: Under ASC 842, a finance lease transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership to the lessee - it meets one of five criteria such as ownership transfer at end of term, a purchase option reasonably certain to be exercised, or a lease term covering most of the asset's useful life. An operating lease does not meet any of those criteria. Both appear on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and lease liability, but the income statement treatment differs: finance leases separate interest expense from amortization, while operating leases record a single straight-line lease cost.

faq.question: How does IFRS 16 differ from ASC 842 in terms of data requirements?
faq.answer: IFRS 16 uses a single lessee model - virtually all leases go on balance sheet with no operating/finance distinction for lessees. The data you need is largely the same (payments, term, discount rate, options), but IFRS 16 requires a lessee's incremental borrowing rate in the currency of the lease, and the standard is more prescriptive about how to assess extension options. IFRS 16 also requires remeasurement disclosures when there is a lease modification or a reassessment of the lease term.

faq.question: Can I use AI lease abstraction to extract ASC 842 data automatically?
faq.answer: Yes. Tools like Lextract extract the specific fields required for ASC 842 and IFRS 16 compliance - lease term, payment schedule, escalation clauses, renewal options, and termination rights - directly from your PDF lease documents. Automated extraction reduces the risk of manual transcription errors, which are the most common source of incorrect ROU asset and lease liability calculations. The output is structured data ready to feed into your lease accounting system.

title: Data-Driven Commercial Lease Negotiation: What the Numbers Tell You
description: Abstract the lease before you sign it. Here is how structured lease data gives tenant representatives and landlords better negotiating outcomes.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: What lease data gives tenants the most negotiating leverage?
faq.answer: The highest-value data points for tenant negotiation are the CAM cap structure (controllable vs. uncontrollable expense caps limit your long-term exposure), the renewal option rent mechanism (fair market value with floor vs. fixed escalation determines your cost at expiration), the TI allowance relative to actual build-out costs, and free rent periods. These provisions often have a larger total economic impact than the headline base rent - yet most negotiations focus almost entirely on rent per square foot.

faq.question: Should I abstract a lease before or after signing?
faq.answer: Before. Abstracting the letter of intent or lease draft before execution lets you quantify the full economic value of the deal - not just the rent. You can model total cost of occupancy over the full term, compare renewal option economics against current market rates, identify CAM exposure relative to controllable expense caps, and spot provisions that appear standard but have unusual economic effects. After signing, abstraction is still valuable for administration, but you have lost the ability to negotiate out unfavorable terms.

faq.question: How do landlords use lease data in negotiations?
faq.answer: Sophisticated landlords track every concession across their portfolio: TI allowances granted, months of free rent, base rent discounts, and CAM caps. When a tenant requests a concession, the landlord's team can immediately reference comparable deals to determine whether the request is within market range. Tenants who show up with structured data on comparable transactions and a clear model of total cost of occupancy are better positioned to negotiate - because they are speaking the same data language the landlord's team uses internally.

faq.question: What is a letter of intent and what data should it include?
faq.answer: A letter of intent (LOI) is a non-binding term sheet that captures the economic outline of a lease before the full lease document is drafted. At minimum it should specify the premises square footage, base rent and escalation structure, lease term and commencement date, renewal options and renewal rent mechanism, TI allowance, free rent period, and parking ratio. Omitting any of these from the LOI forces them to be negotiated during lease drafting, when the tenant has less leverage because they have often already committed to the space.

title: Commercial Lease Administration: A Workflow Guide for Property Managers
description: From lease execution to expiration, here is how professional lease administrators manage the full lifecycle of a commercial lease.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: What should be abstracted from a lease immediately after execution?
faq.answer: The first week after execution is the most critical window for lease administration. Abstract the material economic terms before any data entry into your property management system: commencement and expiration dates, full rent schedule with escalation dates, all option rights and their notice windows, CAM structure and caps, security deposit details, and tenant improvement allowance disbursement terms. Getting this data right at the start prevents errors that compound over the entire lease term - incorrect rent schedules and missed notice deadlines are almost always traceable to poor initial abstraction.

faq.question: How should rent escalations be tracked and billed correctly?
faq.answer: Rent escalations should be entered into your property management system as scheduled future charges at the point of lease setup, not updated manually when the escalation date arrives. Most property management systems support future-dated rent schedules. Manually updating rent at escalation time creates a dependency on someone remembering to do it - and that is where billing errors originate. Verify that your abstracted escalation schedule matches what is in the system at lease execution, then audit it again at each escalation date.

faq.question: What is the correct process for handling a lease amendment?
faq.answer: When a lease amendment is executed, re-abstract only the sections that changed - do not re-abstract the entire lease unless the amendment substantially rewrites it. Document which provisions were amended, effective when, and update your property management system and critical dates calendar to reflect the changes. Keep both the original lease and all amendments in your document repository; the amendment controls, but you need the base lease to interpret terms the amendment did not address. Never delete or overwrite the pre-amendment data - maintain version history.

faq.question: What are the most common lease administration mistakes that lead to financial losses?
faq.answer: The most costly mistakes are missed renewal option deadlines (which forfeit below-market renewal rights), failure to send timely move-out notices (which trigger holdover penalties), unbilled rent escalations (which create revenue leakage that is difficult to recover retroactively), and failure to audit CAM reconciliations within the lease's audit window. All of these are preventable with systematic lease abstraction and a maintained critical dates calendar. The root cause in almost every case is relying on manual processes or spreadsheets rather than structured lease data.

title: Data Security and Compliance in Lease Abstraction
description: How to protect sensitive lease data during abstraction. Covers PII handling, access controls, vendor security, and compliance requirements for CRE firms.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

sources.title: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)
sources.publisher: California Office of the Attorney General

sources.title: 16 CFR Part 314 - Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information
NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology

faq.question: What personally identifiable information is commonly found in commercial leases?
faq.answer: Commercial leases regularly contain guarantor names and home addresses, Social Security numbers in personal guarantee exhibits, dates of birth, and financial statements attached as exhibits to demonstrate creditworthiness. Corporate leases may also include officers' personal financial information when the landlord required personal guarantees. This PII is subject to state privacy laws including CCPA in California, and firms handling it must treat it with the same controls they would apply to any other category of sensitive personal data.

faq.question: What security controls should I require from a lease abstraction vendor?
faq.answer: At minimum, require SOC 2 Type II certification (which covers security, availability, and confidentiality), data encryption in transit (TLS 1.2 or higher) and at rest (AES-256), role-based access controls with multi-factor authentication, a clear data retention and deletion policy, and a signed data processing agreement that limits how the vendor can use your data. For portfolios containing sensitive tenant financial information, also verify that the vendor does not use your documents to train AI models without consent.

faq.question: Do I need to notify tenants if their lease data is abstracted by a third party?
faq.answer: It depends on your jurisdiction and the nature of the data. For institutional portfolios operating under standard commercial terms, lease abstraction for internal administration typically falls under routine business operations and does not trigger tenant notification requirements. However, if you are abstracting leases containing personal guarantees with PII and sharing that data with third-party service providers, review your state's privacy regulations. California's CCPA, for example, requires disclosure of third-party data sharing for certain categories of personal information.

faq.question: How should lease documents be stored and disposed of securely?
faq.answer: Lease PDFs and extracted data should be stored in access-controlled repositories with audit logging that records who accessed each document and when. Retention periods should match your lease terms plus any applicable statute of limitations for disputes - typically the lease term plus 7 years. When deleting data, use cryptographic erasure for cloud-stored files or certified destruction for physical documents. Define these policies in writing before you start an abstraction project, not after the data is already distributed across multiple systems.

title: Commercial Lease Renewal and Termination: A Legal Reference Guide
description: A legal reference guide to commercial lease renewals and terminations. Covers notice periods, option types, holdover provisions, and negotiation tactics.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: How far in advance do I need to exercise a lease renewal option?
faq.answer: Most commercial leases require 6 to 12 months' written notice to exercise a renewal option. Larger deals and longer lease terms often require 12 to 18 months. Missing the deadline is not a minor issue because renewal options are usually enforced according to the notice mechanics written in the lease. Track renewal notice deadlines in a calendar system with reminders set 90 days before the deadline, not 30.

faq.question: What happens if I stay in the space after my lease expires?
faq.answer: If you remain in possession after the lease term expires without exercising a renewal option or executing a new lease, you enter holdover status. Most commercial leases specify holdover rent at 125% to 150% of the last month's rent, with some setting it as high as 200%. The holdover period may create either a month-to-month tenancy or a tenancy at sufferance depending on your lease language. Either way, it creates uncertainty for both parties and can expose the tenant to liability if the landlord had committed the space to another tenant.

faq.question: What is a lease termination fee and how is it calculated?
faq.answer: A lease termination fee is the payment a tenant makes to exit a lease early under a negotiated termination right. The most common calculation methods are unamortized TI allowance plus unamortized leasing commissions (the landlord recoups their upfront investment), several months of base rent (typically 3–6 months in shorter-term leases), or a combination of both. The fee compensates the landlord for the economic value of the remaining lease term while allowing the tenant to exit. Termination rights are negotiated at lease execution - you generally cannot add them afterward without the landlord's agreement.

faq.question: What is the difference between a renewal option and a right of first refusal?
faq.answer: A renewal option gives the tenant the unilateral right to extend the lease for a defined additional term at terms specified in (or determinable under) the lease. A right of first refusal (ROFR) gives the tenant the right to match any bona fide offer the landlord receives from a third party to lease the space. A renewal option is more valuable because the tenant controls the timing; a ROFR is contingent on the landlord finding another interested tenant. Both must be tracked as critical dates since both have notice requirements and expiration windows.

title: Lease Abstraction for Portfolio Management: Scaling from 10 to 1,000 Leases
description: How property managers and asset managers scale lease abstraction across large portfolios. Covers data standards, critical dates, and technology decisions.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: At what portfolio size should I stop using spreadsheets for lease management?
faq.answer: The practical limit for spreadsheet-based lease management is around 20–30 leases for a single person, or 50–75 leases across a small team with clear ownership. Beyond that, version control breaks down, critical date tracking becomes error-prone, and the rent roll is never quite current. The transition point is not purely about volume - it is about the risk of a missed deadline or billing error exceeding the cost of a proper system. For most organizations, that tipping point comes well before 100 leases.

faq.question: What fields should every lease abstract include for portfolio management?
faq.answer: A portfolio-grade lease abstract should capture at minimum: tenant name, premises address and suite, rentable square footage, lease commencement and expiration dates, base rent schedule with escalation dates and amounts, all renewal and termination options with their exercise windows, CAM structure and any expense caps, security deposit amount and conditions for return, and any co-tenancy or exclusivity provisions. These 10–12 data categories cover the majority of administrative decisions a property manager makes over the lease term.

faq.question: How do I standardize lease data across leases drafted by different attorneys?
faq.answer: The key is to define your data dictionary before you start abstracting - a fixed list of fields with precise definitions of what each field captures and how edge cases are handled. For example, 'lease expiration date' needs a definition that addresses how to handle leases that expire on option exercise vs. original term. Once the dictionary exists, the same definition applies regardless of how the underlying lease is drafted. AI-based abstraction tools like Lextract apply a consistent field schema across every lease, which eliminates the inconsistencies that arise when different team members abstract the same portfolio.

faq.question: What is a critical dates calendar and how should it be managed?
faq.answer: A critical dates calendar tracks every date in the portfolio that triggers an obligation or right: renewal notice deadlines, termination option windows, rent escalation dates, lease expiration dates, CAM reconciliation deadlines, and option exercise periods. Best practice is to set automated reminders at 12 months, 6 months, and 90 days before each deadline. The calendar should be generated from the abstracted lease data - not maintained manually - so that when a lease is amended, the calendar updates automatically rather than relying on someone to remember to update it.

title: Understanding Commercial Lease Financial Terms: Base Rent to Percentage Rent
description: A complete reference for commercial lease financial terms. Covers base rent, escalations, NNN vs gross, TI allowances, and percentage rent with examples.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: What is the difference between a gross lease and a NNN lease?
faq.answer: In a gross lease, the tenant pays a single all-in rent amount and the landlord covers most or all operating expenses including taxes, insurance, and maintenance. In a triple-net (NNN) lease, the tenant pays base rent plus their pro-rata share of property taxes, building insurance, and all maintenance costs. NNN leases give tenants more transparency into actual operating costs but also expose them to expense volatility. Modified gross leases fall between the two extremes, with the lease specifying exactly which expenses each party pays.

faq.question: How is a rent escalation clause calculated?
faq.answer: The three most common escalation structures are fixed percentage increases (e.g., 3% annually), CPI-indexed increases tied to the Consumer Price Index for a specific metro area, and fixed dollar step-ups at defined intervals. Fixed percentages are the simplest to model - a $30 PSF base rent with 3% annual escalations reaches $34.84 PSF by year five. CPI escalations are unpredictable but common in longer-term leases. Always check whether the escalation compounds or is calculated on the original base rent.

faq.question: What is a tenant improvement allowance and how does it work?
faq.answer: A tenant improvement (TI) allowance is a landlord contribution - usually expressed as a dollar amount per rentable square foot - toward the cost of building out the space to the tenant's specifications. The landlord either pays contractors directly or reimburses the tenant after construction. TI allowances above what is actually spent typically revert to the landlord, not the tenant. The economic value of a TI allowance depends on the construction costs in your market, so a $50 PSF TI in a low-cost market is worth far more than $50 PSF in an expensive urban market.

faq.question: What is percentage rent and which lease types use it?
faq.answer: Percentage rent is an additional rent component paid when a retail tenant's gross sales exceed a breakpoint amount defined in the lease. For example, a lease might specify 6% of annual sales above $1,000,000 in addition to the base rent. Percentage rent is almost exclusively used in retail leases - particularly in shopping centers - because it aligns the landlord's income with the tenant's business performance. Office and industrial leases rarely include percentage rent provisions.

title: The CRE Professional's Guide to CAM Reconciliation and Audit Rights
description: A practical guide to CAM reconciliation for commercial tenants and property managers. Covers audit rights, common overcharges, and dispute resolution.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

sources.title: Mastering CAM Audits: A Comprehensive Guide to Ensuring Fair Charges and Optimizing Costs

faq.question: How long do I have to audit my CAM reconciliation statement?
faq.answer: Most commercial leases give tenants 12 months after receiving the annual CAM reconciliation statement to object or request an audit. Some leases shorten this to 90 days, and a few extend it to 24 months. If you miss the deadline, you typically waive your right to dispute that year's charges - even if the landlord overcharged you. Read your lease's audit rights clause before your statement arrives, not after.

faq.question: What are the most common CAM overcharges I should look for?
faq.answer: The most frequent overcharges include capital expenditures improperly billed as operating expenses, landlord management fees that exceed the lease's stated cap, depreciation of owner-paid improvements included in operating costs, costs excluded under the lease (such as leasing commissions or top-floor tenant costs) that are included anyway, and base year errors that inflate the variable portion of gross leases. CAM audit guidance from Mohr Partners describes invoice, contract, and allocation review as the practical way to find charge categories that do not match the lease.

faq.question: What does a CAM audit actually involve?
faq.answer: A CAM audit is a review of the landlord's actual invoices, contracts, and general ledger to verify that the charges on your reconciliation statement match allowable expenses under the lease. You (or your CPA or lease audit firm) compare each line item against the lease's definition of operating expenses, check the allocation methodology against the lease's pro-rata share formula, and verify that excluded costs are not included. The process typically takes 4–8 weeks and requires the landlord to produce supporting documentation.

faq.question: Can I recover the cost of a CAM audit if I find overcharges?
faq.answer: Many leases include a provision that requires the landlord to reimburse the tenant's audit costs if the audit uncovers overcharges above a threshold - commonly 5% of the amounts in dispute. If your lease does not include this provision, audit cost recovery is negotiable at renewal. Even without recovery, the economics depend on the lease, the size of the disputed charges, and whether the audit identifies recoverable errors.
